data.title: House Robber II
data.summary:
Input: nums, a list of non-negative integers representing money in houses arranged in a circle.
Output: Maximum amount of money you can rob tonight without alerting the police by robbing two adjacent houses.
Rules: The first house is adjacent to the last house.

data.key_insight: Because the houses are arranged in a circle, the first and last houses cannot be robbed together. This breaks the circle into two linear subproblems: either we can consider houses from index 0 to n-2 (excluding the last house), or from index 1 to n-1 (excluding the first house). The maximum of these two linear House Robber problems is our answer.

steps.title: Handle Edge Case
steps.detail: If there is only one house, simply return the amount in that house. If there are two houses, return the maximum of the two.

steps.title: Define Linear Robber Function
steps.detail: Create a helper function that solves the standard House Robber problem for a linear array of houses using dynamic programming with constant space.

steps.title: Solve Subproblem 1
steps.detail: Run the linear robber function on the houses excluding the last one: nums[:-1].

steps.title: Solve Subproblem 2
steps.detail: Run the linear robber function on the houses excluding the first one: nums[1:].

steps.title: Combine Results
steps.detail: Return the maximum of the two subproblem results.

events.detail: Pattern: Dynamic Programming with Subproblems · 3 hints

data.pattern_summary: Breaking a complex problem into smaller overlapping linear subproblems and combining their results. Reach for this when a constraint (like a circle) prevents applying a standard linear approach directly.

pattern_options.name: Dynamic Programming with Subproblems
pattern_options.feedback: Correct. The circular layout forces us to split the problem into two separate linear house robber subproblems.

pattern_options.name: Two pointers
pattern_options.feedback: Incorrect. Two pointers track ranges moving inward or outward, which does not easily handle non-adjacent combination choices here.

pattern_options.name: Greedy algorithm
pattern_options.feedback: Incorrect. Taking the locally largest amount at each step will miss optimal combinations across the entire sequence.

pattern_options.name: Backtracking
pattern_options.feedback: Incorrect. While backtracking explores all subsets, it results in exponential time without taking advantage of optimal substructure.

signals.hint: Implies that the ends are connected, breaking standard linear algorithms.

signals.phrase: without alerting the police by robbing two adjacent houses
signals.hint: Indicates a constraint on neighboring choices that restricts valid combinations.

data.brute_force_idea: Generate every possible subset of houses, check if any adjacent houses are robbed together, and find the maximum sum among the valid subsets for both the sliced ranges.
data.brute_force_why: Using bitmasks to generate all subsets for an array of length n takes 2^n operations, repeating checks for every subset.
data.bottleneck: Checking every single subset combination using bitmasks, which recalculates sums and checks validity for combinations that overlap significantly.
bottleneck_hints: Look at how many subsets are being generated and tested.
Notice that decisions at one house depend only on the immediate neighbors.
Think about how solving a smaller prefix of houses could help build the answer for the next house without checking all subsets.

events.label: Coach: why the complexity is what it is

data.insight: The circular constraint means the first and last houses cannot be robbed together. By breaking the circle into two separate linear problems—one excluding the last house and one excluding the first house—we eliminate the adjacency wrap-around and reuse the standard linear house robber dynamic programming solution.

derivation.note: The loop runs once for each house in the subproblem array of length approximately n.
Constant time max calculation executed once per house.
Constant time variable reassignment executed once per house.
Constant time variable reassignment executed once per house.

data.time_summary: The helper function rob_linear runs in O(n) time due to the single loop over the array. The main function calls rob_linear twice (once for nums[:-1] and once for nums[1:]), resulting in O(2n) operations, which simplifies to O(n) time overall as verified by the linear growth of steps in the measured evidence.
data.space_summary: The solution uses a fixed number of scalar variables (prev_two, prev_one, current) to track the state instead of an array, requiring O(1) auxiliary space.
data.takeaway: When faced with a circular data structure, break it down into a small number of overlapping linear subproblems where the boundary conditions are explicitly forced or forbidden.
mistakes: Failing to handle arrays of length 1 or 2 as special cases, leading to index out of bounds or incorrect subproblem slicing.
Forgetting that slicing creates shallow copies that take O(n) time and space if not managed carefully.
Attempting to solve the circular constraint with a single pass instead of splitting into two distinct linear checks.

events.label: Tutor: build the visual explanation

data.overview: House Robber II solves the circular street problem by breaking it into two linear subproblems. Since the first and last houses are adjacent and cannot be robbed together, we compute the maximum loot by either excluding the last house or excluding the first house.
data.intuition: Imagine a necklace of pearls (houses) where the clasp connects the first and last pearl. To find the most valuable combination of non-adjacent pearls without opening the clasp, you evaluate the chain twice: once without the last pearl, and once without the first pearl.
